irwin: Oh! You came to talk to ME. Okay. Okay okay okay. Here is what I know.
I have been waiting all evening for someone to ask.
I will tell you everything. I am incapable of anything else.
First — and this is important — you are doing a wonderful job.
I saw something. I have been carrying it around like a stick.
boo: Closer. I won't say it loudly.
granolia: Oh darling, sit, sit — you will not BELIEVE.
I've been dying to tell someone, and you have kind eyes.
Now I only know what I saw, but what I saw was PLENTY.
Between us — and I mean that, between us and whoever else asks —
zimothy: I'll be brief. Brevity is free.
I keep records. The records keep everyone else honest.
You want information. Information has value. Luckily for you, I'm feeling charitable.
Per my ledger — and my ledger does not lie —
I noticed it the way I notice everything: itemized.
salem: Finally. Someone with the sense to consult the only competent investigator here.
I have solved it. Sit down.
What I am about to tell you, I have verified personally, using methods.
The others will give you facts. I give you TRUTH.
I was there. In a sense. In the truest sense.

irwin: That is everything. I feel much lighter.
I hope that helps. I hope everything helps.
If you learn more, come tell me. I will act surprised.
You may pet me now. For your trouble.
I would never lie to you. I don't know how it's done.
boo: Don't quote me. Or do. It was true.
granolia: But you didn't hear it from me, dear. Officially.
Isn't it AWFUL? I've told everyone.
Of course my memory isn't what it was. It was never what it was.
Now off you go — and send someone else over, I'm on a roll.
I'd swear to it. On somebody's grave. There's a fresh one, I hear.
zimothy: Verify it if you like. Verification is billed separately.
The rest is in the ledger, and the ledger is not for browsing.
You'll find I'm rarely wrong. It would be too expensive.
salem: You may thank me for solving this.
Nobody listens to the cat. History will.
Cross-reference it if you must. It will hold. It always holds.
I'd stake my ninth life on it. The others are spoken for.
Tell no one. Tell everyone. It changes nothing — I am right.

echo_frames: ...residents further report ███. Authorities have declined to comment...
...staff describe ███, though none would be quoted directly...
...witnesses recall ███. The household maintains that all is well...
...this station has received word of ███. More as the situation develops...
...rumors persist regarding ███. The vicar urges calm...

templates.name: Receipt
templates.brief: Shop letterhead, itemized lines, total box

templates.name: Telegram
templates.brief: Office banner, delivery stamps, gummed message strip

templates.name: Household notice
templates.brief: Pinned handbill, slightly askew, torn corner

templates.name: Citation / form
templates.brief: Official numbering, field lines, RECEIVED stamp

templates.name: Personal letter
templates.brief: Writing paper, margin room for a second ink

templates.name: Playbill
templates.brief: Ornate border, artwork zone text can deface

opener.what: The FIRST sentence of a cat's testimony — spoken before any information. Pure personality, zero facts.
opener.test: Would it make sense in front of ANY secret?
examples: Shut the door. This stays between us and the fireplace.
I wasn't going to say anything. That lasted an hour.

closer.what: The LAST sentence — the sign-off after the information lands. Deflection, running gag, mic drop.
closer.test: Would it make sense after ANY secret?
examples: And that is the last I'll speak of it. Until asked again.
Now if you'll excuse me, the sunbeam is moving.

echo_frame.what: A news-broadcast wrapper. You write the announcer's sentence; the sealed fragment fills the ███.
echo_frame.test: Read it in a radio voice — the ███ sits where the juicy part goes.
examples: ...neighbors speak of ███, though never above a whisper...
...the constable was asked about ███ and chose to examine his boots...

room.what: Rooms of the manor — dropped in as WHERE it happened.
room.test: Any Victorian-sounding room pairs with any incident.
examples: the conservatory
the wine cellar
the servants' stair

time.what: Times of day — dropped in as WHEN it happened.
time.test: Proper o'clock or dramatic vagueness, both useful.
examples: half past luncheon
the stroke of nine
whilst decent folk slept

duration.test: Absurdly short and absurdly long are both funny.
examples: the better part of a sermon
one unforgivable instant
a fortnight
once — once was enough
nine times, as if practiced
thirteen

place.what: Spots OUT IN TOWN — shops, venues, institutions.
place.test: Anywhere a Victorian could have a bad day in public.
examples: the haberdasher's
the opera house
the fishmonger's queue

crowd.test: From one soul to all of society — range helps the shuffle.
examples: the entire choir
a visiting bishop
two maids and a startled gardener

refusal.what: What the screen shows when a cat WON'T talk to you: Boo below affection 4, Zimothy stonewalling the wrong profession, a rationed short-version register. Per docs/cat-info.md, Boo's refusals read personal (guarded, not snobbish); Zimothy's read professional.
refusal.test: Does it sting, stay in register, and hint that a way in exists — without giving information?
examples: Zimothy: I don't discuss accounts with the accountless. The Banker may inquire on your behalf.
Boo: (She looks past you, at absolutely nothing, which is somehow worse.)

smalltalk.what: Fact-free ambient lines for room screens — complaints, observations, running gags. They shuffle in beside clue lines, so they must carry ZERO case information. Some can quietly teach the cat's public nature (the room learning 'Salem gets things backwards').
smalltalk.test: Could this line appear in any game, any night, and spoil nothing?
examples: Salem: The east hedge is winning. I've let it think so.
Granolia: I alphabetized the atlas today. *snrk.* It was already alphabetized. Best day of my life.

trailoff.what: Granolia's forget-connectives. Her testimony omits exactly one detail — these lines are the splice that papers over the hole, in her canon register (snorting study nerd, honest, zero malice).
trailoff.test: Would it read naturally where a missing WHERE, WHEN, or HOW MANY should be?
examples: — oh, it's gone. It was just here. The thought, not the thing.
...and, hm. *snrk.* I want to say Tuesday? Don't write that down.

status_line.what: PRIVATE per-player lines about where you stand with a cat, by tier: locked out, warming, in. Relationship only — never case content. (Per docs/cat-info.md: your device only.)
status_line.test: Does it convey standing without leaking what the cat knows?
examples: Boo hasn't decided about you yet.
Salem approves of anyone with honest calluses. You appear to qualify.

npc_card.what: The public meet-the-household card for one of the five animals: name, canon title, 2–3 sentences of personality, where in the manor they're found. Hints at their nature without stating the mechanic — and NEVER remarks that they talk.
npc_card.test: Read it aloud: does it introduce a household member, not a game feature?
examples: SALEM CROOKNOG — the long-time groundskeeper. Been here longer than the hedges, and rates them higher than you. Ask him anything; he is never in doubt.
GRANOLIA LICKSPITTLE — taken in by the family when no one else would. Keeps to the study. Knows plenty. Remembers... most.

bio.what: One player character: pun name, profession, a paragraph of persona, a costume nudge. Professions are load-bearing — they seed cat affection and Zimothy's class gate. Must stay motive-agnostic: anyone can be Murderer, Ghost, or victim.
bio.test: Could an 11-year-old and a 70-year-old each play this person after one read?
examples: REV. BARKLEY BUNSWORTH — the Baker. Flour on his cuffs, scripture in one pocket, scones in the other...
MAJ. WHISKERTON PLUME (RET.) — the Sergeant Major. Has opinions about posture. Salutes the dog.

lore.what: The household bible: canon paragraphs every other surface quotes. The Sirwin family (names for Mama, Papa, the siblings), how each cat came to the manor, the unknown-victim premise (how a murder is known with no body named), Sir Irwin's register entry.
lore.test: If two screens both mention this fact, do they agree because they both quote THIS?
examples: THE INCIDENT: At the stroke of the blackout, a murder most certain occurred at Sirwin Manor. The household knows it in its bones. Who was taken? The Manor is not yet ready to say...
SIR IRWIN: the birthday boy. Family, not staff. Incapable of untruth; unclear on the concept.

rules.what: One rulebook section per item: the premise, the win condition (name Murderer + Motive + Victim), the seven acts, talking to cats, documents and echoes, using your phone, the motive menu, events, Spill-the-Beans. Short. Plain. Victorian garnish optional.
rules.test: One read, ages 11 and 70, no follow-up questions.
examples: HOW YOU WIN — By the end of the night, name three things: who did it, why, and to whom. Everyone plays. Everyone can win. Yes, everyone.
THE CATS — The household will speak to you. Some more honestly than others. Compare notes; the truth is a group project.

ui_copy.what: System strings, one per item, labeled by surface: join/QR flow, lobby, motive-menu chrome, kiosk idle text, ballot + confirmation, results variants, rejoin/offline/waiting states, act countdowns, journal labels, help lines. Prefix each with its surface in CAPS.
ui_copy.test: Would a stressed 70-year-old on a locked phone understand this string alone?
examples: REJOIN: The Manor remembers you. Take your seat — nothing was lost.
BALLOT CONFIRM: Once sealed, an accusation cannot be unsaid. Speak now?

role_card.what: The Act 1 blackout copy: the shared buzz message, then the Murderer / Ghost / innocent cards (matched in length so lit screens give no tells), then the two fuller hidden-role briefings. Nobody learns the motive — the cards must say so.
role_card.test: Glanceable in the dark; reveals nothing to a shoulder-surfer beyond its owner's role.
examples: INNOCENT: You are exactly who you say you are. Tonight that makes you rare. Find the truth before it finds you.
MURDERER: It was you. You know how. You do not know WHY — even you will need the motive. Keep your face kind.

event_card.what: The menu hidden roles pick from: Victorian-flavored name + plain effect line. Effects touch information VOLUME and TIMING only, never content, and obey 'delay, never destroy' — anything suppressed resurfaces in Act 4. Include which acts the card is legal in.
event_card.test: Does the effect line mention only volume/timing? Could the card spoil anything? (It must not.)
examples: A DREADFUL DRAUGHT (Act 2) — One room's cat says nothing this act. What it withheld arrives in Act 4.
THE POST IS LATE (Act 2/4) — The next echo is delayed one act. It arrives unaltered.

epilogue_frame.what: The 'and so it was...' narration for after the third reveal — a full story frame with slots the runtime fills: [MURDERER], [VICTIM], the motive rhyme, the document's tell, pool variables. You write every word; the night fills the blanks.
epilogue_frame.test: Read aloud with placeholder names — does it land as the story of the whole evening?
examples: And so it was [MURDERER] all along — undone by [MOTIVE_RHYME], as the paper trail whispered from the very first...
...and [VICTIM], dear [VICTIM], never saw the teatime coming.

act_script.what: Per act: the banner/title, the objective blurb players see, and the host run-of-show beats (gather/disperse call, cue firing order, rough timing, lines Jon performs). All blind-safe — no step may depend on knowing the case.
act_script.test: Could Jon-the-player follow this script all night and learn nothing?
examples: BANNER: Act the Second — In Which Everyone Minds Their Own Business, Poorly.
BEAT: Fire 'disperse' chime → announce 'the household will receive you now' → four rooms, one cat each.

ops_doc.what: One host-side document per item: welcome speech, Susan's Detective briefing, Stream Deck cue sheet, room map + kiosk placement, night-of contingency sheet, pre-party tech checklist, canary ask + rubric, rehearsal plan, invitation + guest instructions, puzzle input specs. Title in CAPS, then the doc.
ops_doc.test: Spoiler-safe (Jon reads all of these) and usable mid-party at a glance.
examples: SUSAN BRIEFING: If anyone says 'wait, the cat talks?' you answer as though asked about a person. 'Mr. Crooknog? He's been here forty years.' Never more.
TECH CHECKLIST: Fire every cue in DUMMY MODE first. Generate the real case LAST, after all kiosk checks.

art_asset.what: Every piece of art the night needs, tracked as a checklist. Check items off as they're finished; add notes or new items freely. Reference uploads land here when the stationery tracker ships.
art_asset.test: If every box were checked, would every screen at the party look finished?
examples: Portrait — Miss Boo LaRue (flapper, mid-decision about you)
Kiosk chrome — idle state

av_asset.what: Every sound and moving image, tracked as a checklist. Canon rule: audio is generic atmosphere ONLY — chimes, crackle, thunder — never spoken information. Wordless by design.
av_asset.test: Could any clip leak information if played at the wrong moment? (It must not be able to.)
examples: Blackout sting (power-cut)
Echo broadcast bed — static, tuning squeal, attention chime
